passage:
In Kasba Road College, the back bench of Class 11 had its own language. Keerthana and Zubin and three others called the bus conductor "Captain Jugaad," did a slow clap whenever a teacher said "to sum up," and used the word "paneer" to mean "I'm bored." Keerthana loved it. When the group laughed at her jokes, something in her chest loosened.
Then a new girl, Shruti, sat beside them and asked, "What's paneer?" Zubin smirked. "You wouldn't get it." Keerthana laughed with him before she'd even thought.
Later she saw Shruti eating lunch alone, and the laugh sat in her stomach like a stone. The next day she told Shruti, "It's just our silly code. Want to know the rest?"

qa.q: What nickname did the back bench give the bus conductor?
qa.a: They called the bus conductor "Captain Jugaad."

qa.q: How did Keerthana feel when the group laughed at her jokes?
qa.a: Keerthana felt included and relieved, as though something in her chest loosened.

qa.q: What did Keerthana do that turned the inside jokes from a wall into a door?
qa.a: The next day Keerthana told Shruti it was just their silly code and offered to share the rest. That let Shruti in.

qa.q: How might Shruti have felt when Zubin smirked and said she would not get it?
qa.a: Shruti was probably embarrassed and left out, and she was later seen eating lunch alone.

grounding: A teenager uses inside jokes to belong, notices they can exclude a new person, and opens the joke up.

The group chat pinged. Sami sent a meme of a cat in a tiny hat, captioned "Mr Patel's face when we said Friday." Six people replied with laughing reactions and a string of 😅. It was the fastest thing Sami had felt all week: a small click of belonging.
In the hallway, Freya, who had joined the school in September, said, "I don't get the Mr Patel thing. Why is it funny?"
Sami opened his mouth to explain, but Dan behind him said, "You had to be there," and everyone snickered. Sami snickered too, then looked at Freya's face and felt a small drop in his chest.
That night he sent Freya a private message: "Sorry about earlier. The Mr Patel thing is a long story, want it? 🙂"

qa.q: What was the caption on Sami's meme?
qa.a: The caption was "Mr Patel's face when we said Friday."

qa.q: What did Sami feel when the group chat replied with laughing reactions?
qa.a: Sami felt a small click of belonging, as if he was part of the group.

qa.q: What did Sami do that evening to fix the moment in the hallway?
qa.a: Sami sent Freya a private message apologising and offering to explain the Mr Patel joke. It gave Freya a way into the group.

qa.q: What is it like for Freya to hear "You had to be there" when Freya asked about the joke?
qa.a: Freya is probably left out and a little embarrassed, being new since September. A joke that is not shared can make the group feel closed.

grounding: A teenager uses memes to bond with peers, notices a newcomer excluded by them, and reaches out.

passage:
In Class 11 in Aizawl, our group spoke in jokes. "Chicken or egg?" meant someone was about to lie. A picture of a sad potato meant exam stress. We'd been building them since Class 7, and I loved it. Walking into class and getting a joke from across the room felt like belonging.
Then Lalremsiami joined in July. She sat with us at lunch, and we kept saying "chicken or egg" and laughing, and she kept looking from face to face. On the third day she sat with someone else.
That night I felt awful. Our jokes felt like home to me, and I'd never noticed they could be a closed door.
The next day I went and sat with her. "Okay, sad potato. Let me explain." She laughed at the potato. Now she's the one sending it. I'm Bhupen, by the way, and I still love our jokes.

qa.q: What did a picture of a sad potato mean in the group?
qa.a: It meant exam stress.

qa.q: What was Bhupen feeling the night Lalremsiami sat elsewhere?
qa.a: Bhupen felt awful and guilty, realising the jokes that felt like home had shut someone out.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Sitting with Lalremsiami and explaining the sad potato worked, because it opened the inside joke to her instead of using it as a wall.

qa.q: What was lunch like for Lalremsiami in her first days?
qa.a: She probably felt confused and left out, looking from face to face while everyone laughed at jokes she didn't know.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose group bonds through inside jokes, noticing that the same jokes can shut out a newcomer.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 10B, Friday.
Ramesh's group of five sit at the back and communicate mostly in memes and sarcasm. It's clearly how they bond; they're funny, and the class laughs with them. This week I noticed something else. When Ritu offered an idea in the group project, Ramesh said, "Wow, groundbreaking," and the others burst into their private joke, a sound like a buzzer. Ritu went quiet and stopped offering ideas for the rest of the week.
I spoke to Ramesh after class. At first he said, "It's just our humour, Ma'am." I asked him who laughs and who doesn't. He thought about it for a while and said, "Ritu doesn't." I asked him to find a way to include her by Monday.
I'll check in with Ritu separately on Monday too.

qa.q: How many students are in Ramesh's group?
qa.a: Five.

qa.q: What was Ramesh thinking when he said it was just their humour?
qa.a: He seemed a little defensive at first, and then uncomfortable as he realised Ritu was not laughing.

qa.q: What did the teacher do next that might help?
qa.a: She asked Ramesh who laughs and who doesn't, gave him a task to include Ritu by Monday, and planned to check in with Ritu too.

qa.q: How did Ritu seem to be affected by the buzzer joke?
qa.a: Ritu went quiet and stopped offering ideas, which suggests she felt hurt and shut out.

grounding: Shows a teenager using sarcasm and inside jokes to bond with friends, and how that humour can also exclude another student.

passage:
Wednesday, 10 pm
Our group chat is basically one long joke. Someone types "mango season" whenever a teacher gets dramatic, and all five of us lose it. It's the best part of my day. When I'm sad I scroll back through it.
Today Kishore got added because he's in our physics project. Within an hour, Ananth started sending "mango season" every time Kishore typed anything. Kishore asked what it meant. Nobody explained. We just kept sending mangoes. 🥭
I laughed. Then I stopped. I remembered being new in Class 8, when nobody explained anything to me either.
The same joke that makes me feel like I belong was being used to show Kishore he doesn't.
I DMed him: "It's a teacher joke, I'll explain tomorrow, it's dumb 😅" He sent back a thumbs up.
Tomorrow I'm going to explain it in the group too.
Mahima

qa.q: What does the group type whenever a teacher gets dramatic?
qa.a: They type 'mango season'.

qa.q: What was Mahima feeling when she stopped laughing?
qa.a: Mahima felt uneasy and a bit guilty, remembering how it felt to be new and left out in Class 8.

qa.q: What small step could Mahima take in the group tomorrow?
qa.a: Mahima could explain the joke to everyone and invite Kishore in, so the humour includes him instead of marking him as an outsider.

qa.q: How might Kishore feel when nobody explained the joke?
qa.a: He was probably confused and left out, sensing the joke was about him.

grounding: Shows a teenager who bonds through a group chat's inside jokes, noticing the same humour being used to exclude a newcomer.
